fixed: digest drops a valid cut when an identical break from a partly single-stranded site sorts first (sticky input ends) [finding 1]: root cause was collectCleavages() merging identical (top,bottom) events BEFORE the per-site 'end' checks in digestLinear(). Now each event (recognition site x cut pair) is checked for applicability first, and only applicable events are merged into one break, credited to the smallest enzyme name. Sites that cannot cut are each reported with their own footprint. Regression tests: EcoRI+BsmBI, the MlyI twin sites (both variants), BsaI+BsmAI.

Identical breaks are merged before the sticky-end check, so a valid cut is silently lost [finding 3]: same root cause and fix as finding 1. Guarded by an independent first-principles model of sticky-ended linear digests (3,703 fuzzed digests identical, 673 shadowed breaks exercised) and by a new pydna oracle group pydna_digests_near_end.json (300 cases, 67 shadowed) plus a near-end part of the live oracle. Both fail on the old code.

Conflict tie-break contradicts the documented rule (zone ties broken by top, not enzyme name) [finding 2]: the walk comparator is now zone start, zone end, enzyme name, then 5' before 3', as documented. ApaI is applied over PspOMI (linear, circular, reverse-complemented, either input order). Breaks are grouped for merging with a separate comparator.

Conflict resolution depends on the strand the molecule is written on (pUC19 vs its reverse complement) [finding 4]: root cause was the walk running 5'->3' along the TOP strand. Each group of conflicting breaks is now walked along a strand chosen from the molecule itself: the strand whose sequence, read 5'->3' outward from the group's centre, sorts first. Linear ends enter that comparison by kind and length. Whole-circle coverage starts at the least rotation of either strand, which also removes the documented origin-dependence limitation. While doing this I found a pre-existing bug in that whole-circle path: it withdrew already-applied breaks at the end of the lap, leaving blockedBy pointing at unapplied breaks and the result not maximal. It now checks against the first applied break during the walk. Verified: 0/29,856 common x commercial pairs differ in sizes on pUC19 and on pBR322 (review: 1,134 / 747), and 0/193,753 commercial pairs differ in fragment count (review: 42 / 8). Permanent tests: the finding's reproductions, all common x commercial pairs on pUC19, every commercial enzyme alone on pUC19/pBR322 (exact mirror), seeded exact mirror/rotation/enzyme-order properties with 25k conflicts, whole-circle cases, and a palindromic molecule with asymmetric sticky ends.

nonCutters(sites, enzymes) returns enzymes that are not in `enzymes` [finding 5]: cuttersWithCount(sites, n, enzymes) now uses the given list as the candidate set (unique names; listed enzymes without sites count 0; enzymes only present in sites are never returned). nonCutters inherits this; TSDoc updated.

digest accepts input ends that cover the whole molecule and returns a fragment with zero base pairs [finding 6]: checkEnds throws 'leave no base pair' when left + right overhang lengths equal L (sum > L keeps the 'longer than the molecule' message). Tested for all six kind combinations and a 1-bp-left boundary case.
summary:
All six findings reproduced as failing regression tests before any fix, and all are fixed. Findings 1 and 3 are one bug, so five root causes. The enzymes module now passes 122/122 tests in about 4 s (it had 100). `tsc --noEmit` reports no errors in my files; its remaining errors are in other agents' files (`seq/stats.test.ts`, `test/review-tmp/*`). The whole core suite has 13 failures, all in `io/snapgene-read` and `primers/*`. No sudo was needed, no shared file or package.json was edited, no dependency was added, and no git operation was run.

**Behaviour changes callers should know about**
- **New conflict rule.** Each group of conflicting breaks is walked 5'->3' along a strand chosen from the sequence around the group, not the top strand. Results are now the same for a molecule and its reverse complement, for any circle origin (including the old whole-circle limitation) and for any enzyme order. Where the molecule is symmetric, both choices give the same physical fragments. The full rule is in the `digest.ts` header and the TSDoc for `SkipReason`.
- **`DigestReport.skipped` lists one entry per site that did not cut.** When a break is skipped, every site that would have made it is listed. A site that cannot cut because of an end is listed even when another site makes the same break (e.g. BsaI straddling a sticky end while BsmAI inside it cuts). The list is sorted by top, bottom, enzyme, site and strand.
- **Whole-circle conflicts.** Applied breaks are no longer withdrawn at the end of the lap, so `blockedBy` always names an applied break.
- **`cuttersWithCount(sites, n, enzymes)`** is now restricted to the given list.
- **Input ends** that leave no base pair now throw an error.

**Oracle additions**
- **New helpers** in `enzymes_common.py`: `pydna_site_check_reliable` and `count_shadowed`.
- **Why the near-end cases are filtered.** pydna 5.5.16's `cutsite_is_valid` looks for the recognition site at `watson - fst5`, which is only correct for top-strand sites. It is wrong for bottom-strand sites and for the second cut of two-cut enzymes. Near-end cases are restricted to configurations where pydna is reliable.
- **Static oracle.** New file `pydna_digests_near_end.json` (300 cases, 264 KB). Regenerating reproduces the seven existing JSON files byte-identically, and the run is deterministic.
- **Live oracle.** New near-end cases are added after the existing seeded ones, so earlier cases are unchanged. Default seed: 160 near-end digests identical to pydna. A sweep of 12 more seeds: about 2,000 near-end and 2,700 regular digests identical.

**Notes**
- Finding 2's stated expected fragments were miscomputed. The correct ApaI products are `AAAGGGCC` (right 3' overhang 4) and `GGCCCAAA`; the tests assert those.
- Performance is fine: at most about 0.5 s on the 4.6 Mb E. coli genome, including FspEI with 190k conflicts.
